speakers: Andrew Beer (Andrew Beer, DBi / Dynamic Beta founder, managed futures ETF)
Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host, Top Traders Unplugged; caption 'Nils Castrolen')
summary: Andrew Beer argues 60/40 was a historical accident of a 20-year bond bubble and presents six statistical traits of the SG CTA index (crisis alpha, low correlation, alpha, drawdown control, 0.34 Sharpe, lumpy returns). He says the pitch to allocators must change (language, simpler narrative, manager dispersion and no persistence) to take CTAs mainstream.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: It was fueled by the 20-year bond bubble, right? Because bonds were the statistically perfect diversifier to your stock portfolios for 20 years.
claims.claim: 60/40 was a historical accident of the 2000s, fueled by a 20-year bond bull market in which bonds were a near perfect diversifier for stocks, so extrapolating it forward is a mistake.
claims.testable: yes: stock-bond correlation and bond drawdown by era

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: that's sort of when you see this great inflection point with US economic growth
claims.claim: The dot-com mania lowered the perceived cost of starting businesses in the US, raising entrepreneurial risk tolerance and producing an inflection in US growth.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: unimaginably lowered the barriers to entry to starting new businesses
claims.claim: AI sharply lowers the capital and headcount needed to start a business, which should raise entrepreneurship much as the 1990s did, with large disruption.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: it's truly bizarre that we have people spending hundreds of billions of dollars to provide services almost for free
claims.claim: AI capex of hundreds of billions funds near-free services, so the economics look unusual; the equity market has become one large venture-capital style play on AI.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: that things really are unpredictable. That's the the butterfly wings.
claims.claim: Markets and society are complex adaptive systems where small events (an eviction story leading to an election call) cascade unpredictably, which is why trend following responds rather than forecasts.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the trend barometer finished at 52 uh yesterday which is still pretty strong
claims.claim: The Trend barometer at 52 and SG CTA index +15.88% YTD (October 2026), Stockton trend +15.78%, short-term traders +5.78%, versus MSCI World +13.38% show trend following keeping pace with equities in 2026.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Welcome bonds not doing so well this month not doing so well this year down 36 basis points and down 3.15 for the year
claims.claim: Global bonds are down about 3.15% YTD while the S&P 500 is up almost 15%, with fixed income a main driver for CTAs.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: when the portfolios get concentrated in a single macro theme in 2023, 2022 23 is basically the two-year Treasury. um that kind of drove everything
claims.claim: CTA returns look like two steps forward two back when portfolios concentrate in one macro theme (2022-23 short rates) which then reverses; 2026 had several competing themes.
claims.indicator: portfolio concentration in a single macro theme

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: we've generally seen the best years like 2022 are when three of the four asset classes are working well
claims.claim: The best CTA years have three of four asset classes (equities, rates, FX, commodities) contributing.
claims.testable: yes: breadth of sector contribution vs annual return

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: you're basically buying oil at in the 60s in January
claims.claim: 2026 gains came sequentially from long oil from the 60s, EM equities on an AI theme, and then Treasuries and rates, with offsetting positions in between.
claims.direction: long oil, long EM equities, short/long rates

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: It looks dated because it started with the answer.
claims.claim: (Quoting Nordic report) Portfolios should start from required returns, affordable risks, source of diversification, liquidity and what happens when assumptions fail, rather than from a fixed 60/40 pie.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: it has an enormous amount of what's called recency bias
claims.claim: Asset allocation capital markets assumptions are 10-year predictions of 25-40 assets and their correlations, extrapolated from recent decades, and are always wrong.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: commodities give you equity-like returns over decades with a negative correlation to equities
claims.claim: A late-1990s futures-based commodity return series led allocators to add commodities, but the correlation to equities flipped positive in the mid-2000s, so an in-sample correlation is not a stable allocation rule.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: short period of time when cor when when stocks and bonds had negative correlation and bonds never went down
claims.claim: 60/40 rested on a short historical window of negative stock-bond correlation and bonds that never fell.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: among the worst mistakes an allocator could make
claims.claim: At end-2021 with bonds yielding zero and inflation rising, allocators sold equities (up 28%) to buy bonds, adding at the peak of the bond bubble.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: they get the timing wrong. um they get a bit gunshy and they tend not to come back to the space
claims.claim: Allocators tend to time managed futures badly and not return, so shifting away from 60/40 may take a new generation of CIOs.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: $18 trillion of negative yielding bonds.
claims.claim: In 2020-21, $18 trillion of bonds yielded negative and allocators still added bonds when rebalancing.
claims.conditions: Rebalancing rules into bonds at the peak

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the ethos is is don't do anything fast
claims.claim: Asset allocation models rest on diversification (the free lunch) and not trading tactically, because humans are poor market timers, so the whole portfolio view prevents behavioral losses.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: there is something there's something very human in in in your own money handing you money every month that you can go spend
claims.claim: Investors like bonds for the regular coupon, an emotional rather than real-return reason.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the breakdown in the relationship between stocks and bonds is really challenging the simple easy construct
claims.claim: The stock-bond breakdown pushes investors to replace the bond 40, or part of it, with alternatives.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: you now have close to 27 years of daily data of the average net of fee returns of the big players
claims.claim: The SG CTA index (20 largest managed futures funds, since January 2000) gives ~27 years of daily net returns to study the space as a whole.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: you're trying to reduce the idiosyncratic risk of a given manager and try to look at the space overall
claims.claim: Use the index rather than single managers because the sector is more predictable than any one fund and shows behaviour across environments.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: that data point, that period becomes a key part of how portfolios are constructed for the rest of the decade
claims.claim: In the 2000-02 bust (S&P -40%, Nasdaq -80%) US Agg gained 30%, REITs 49%, gold and GSCI rose and the SG CTA index 26% because the Fed cut to the floor, setting the diversifier playbook.
claims.indicator: US Agg, REITs, gold, GSCI, SG CTA index in 2000-02
claims.direction: bonds, REITs, gold, commodities, CTAs up in equity bear market
claims.conditions: Starting from high interest rates with big Fed cuts

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: So bonds don't go up, but they don't go down.
claims.claim: In the GFC bonds only preserved capital, high yield fell 22%, REITs and commodities (-50%) failed as diversifiers, while the SG CTA index rose 11%.
claims.indicator: bonds, high yield, REITs, commodities, SG CTA in GFC
claims.direction: CTAs up when other diversifiers fail
claims.conditions: Equity bear market with already low rates

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the playbook you developed for the do crisis doesn't really work doesn't work at all in the GFC
claims.claim: Each crisis broke the previous diversifier playbook (2022: bonds -15-20%, REITs -25%, gold flat), while CTAs gained again with oil lifting GSCI, so crisis alpha is the strongest argument for the space.
claims.direction: CTAs up in each of three equity crises

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: managers funds make money when there are big price moves away from consensus basically
claims.claim: Trend following structurally profits from big price moves, buying what doubles and shorting what halves ('contrarian tactical alpha'), so it should do well in a crisis.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it was a different kind of volatility that and hence this is why you diversify right
claims.claim: Volatility strategies worked in Volmageddon 2018 and 2020 but not in 2022, because the volatility was a different kind; no crisis hedge is guaranteed.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the tactical nature of it allows them
claims.claim: Tactical trading controls drawdowns (commodities fell 80% peak to trough) because managed futures do not white-knuckle hold losing assets.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: Equity markets from NASDAQ to emerging markets are going to be between 75 and 85% over time.
claims.claim: Switching among equity styles gives little statistical diversification, whereas bond, REIT and commodity categories have positive correlation to equities.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the 2000s and 2010s was an anomaly and people only looked at that period because they didn't want to look at the uncomfortable truth
claims.claim: The negative stock-bond correlation of 2000-2020 was an anomaly: over 27 years US IG +0.36, REITs 0.65, GSCI 0.3, gold ~0, CTAs slightly negative.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: CTAs as a space have slightly negative correlation
claims.claim: Low correlation to traditional assets is the strongest input for including CTAs in an efficient frontier, regardless of daily sign.
claims.indicator: correlation of SG CTA to equities

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: how much of my my returns are sneakily coming from equity exposure
claims.claim: CTA alpha vs S&P 500 was about 330 bp per year over 27 years (high among hedge fund strategies) and is valuable because of the low correlation; alpha is a measure of hidden equity exposure.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: monthly basis of the sock genics over 27 years is 16%
claims.claim: Max monthly drawdown of SG CTA is 16% vs US Agg 17%, Global Agg 24%, S&P 51%, Nasdaq 81%, REITs 69%, gold 42%, commodities 87%.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the space is not built to hold losing positions with a white knuckle grip
claims.claim: Tactical (trend) rules cut losers, so even if long commodities they would not stay long through an 87% decline: capital preservation.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: The average max draw down of any one of those funds the individual funds is closer to 25%.
claims.claim: Individual funds' max drawdowns are ~25% (13% to high 30s; high 40s including departed funds), so the 16% needs diversification across several funds.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the Bloomberg Dag from 2000 to 2020 the max draw down was under 4%
claims.claim: Bonds had max drawdown <4% in 2000-2020 (central bank policy), so CTA 5-10% drawdowns look bad by comparison; equities always recovered.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: thing which is cutting your losses and getting out then the recovery argument is very theoretical
claims.claim: Recovery narrative (hold equities because they come back) favours buy-and-hold assets over a strategy that exits losses.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the low correlation in the crisis alpha is so valuable if you gave me that product with a zero sharp ratio I'd still buy it
claims.claim: The SG CTA index has a 0.34 net Sharpe (cash +275 bp) comparable to equities and bonds (~0.4), rates 0.46, commodities 0.15-0.2; illiquid assets show higher Sharpe by not marking to market.
claims.indicator: Sharpe ratio of SG CTA index

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the average fee management fee was 1.4% and the average incentive fee was like 14%
claims.claim: The 0.34 Sharpe is after trading costs and 1.4%/14% fees, whereas index Sharpe ratios are free and not investable.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: you're up 13% in this space
claims.claim: Returns are lumpy: +13% in 2008, no gains 2009-13, +16% 2014, flat years, +20% in 2022, below cash for three years, then a good 2026.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the problem with the modest sharp ratio and the lumpiness of returns is that if your if your investment horizon is truly 10 years, then it's fine
claims.claim: Lumpy returns are tolerable for 10-year allocators but hard for quarterly committees and wealth clients.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: there's no persistence of returns
claims.claim: Fund dispersion within CTAs is wide and persistence is absent, so differences are mostly modeling luck, making manager selection hard.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: I'm going to focus on the five that have done well recently
claims.claim: The standard performance-chasing selection of recent top funds does not work given no persistence.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: you look at kind of a reasonable period of bonds, it just doesn't help you
claims.claim: For improving the efficient frontier, bonds currently add little versus stocks alone, while CTAs add diversification.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: you've thrown out the tactical baby with the bathwater
claims.claim: Strategic asset allocation is about 90% right; add tactical/managed futures for the rest, framed in allocator language with examples like crude oil at 60, gold 2100 to 5500 and shorts in Treasuries in Dec 2021.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the amount of airtime that goes into trades or opportunities or positioning that is totally immaterial to the overall results of the portfolio
claims.claim: Wealth-management allocators spend time on narrative themes immaterial to results; clients value the story, so narrative is part of the product.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: we've got the mother of all bond market tantrums building
claims.claim: A bond market tantrum may be building in October 2026 and oil and commodities do not look better structurally.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: you'd have 20 guys go into the GFC. Five of them got it right.
claims.claim: Discretionary tactical timers: 20 managers went into the GFC and five got it right and built large businesses while the other 15 blew up, so tactical timing by humans is dangerous.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: You buy gold at 2100. The signal goes on at 2100.
claims.claim: Trend following is early rather than late: a signal bought gold at 2100 and rode it to 5500.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: We we collectively need to all sit in a room.
claims.claim: Relabel the strategy (contrarian tactical alpha) as private equity/private credit/high yield were relabelled, since 'managed futures' and 'trend following' carry bad connotations.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: there's so much variability and about performance over time
claims.claim: Managers who have recently done well credit model nuances, but allocators cannot evaluate those nuances and differences are mostly noise.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: There's there's a long chain of people that we have to actually collectively
claims.claim: Growth requires a simple story that investment committees, advisers and clients can explain, because most allocators do not care whether a fund trades 150 or 120 contracts.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the mutual fund goes to 14 billion $14.3 billion at the peak
claims.claim: Concentrating a 5% allocation in the single best manager (AQR's mutual fund reached $14.3bn) made the later 20% drawdown and underperformance blamed on the whole space.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: it it tempts people to time the space. which then they further get wrong right
claims.claim: Lumpy positive-not-spectacular alpha tempts investors to time the strategy, and they do it badly (rushing in late).

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: if you want two funds in in this category because you want you want to have double the chance of having a great story to tell in a given year
claims.claim: Use two complementary CTA funds so that at least one tells a good story each year, and judge on a 10-year horizon.
